column2: By worshipping the earthen linga he became an excellent man again: a woman for one month and a man for the next, and so his womanhood was undone.
Then, giving up his kingdom and devoted to Shiva's dharma, wearing Shiva's garb, he attained through devotion the liberation so hard to gain.
His son Pururavas, a great king, was a devout worshipper of Shiva, the god of gods, and his son too worshipped Shiva.
Bharata always performed the great worship of Shiva alone, and Nahusha became a great Shaiva, devoted to the worship of Shiva.
Yayati, through the worship of Shiva, obtained all his desires, and begot five sons devoted to Shiva's dharma.
His sons, headed by Yadu, all five of them worshippers of Shiva, obtained all their desires by the power of Shiva's worship.
Others too, most fortunate ones of their line and of other lines, worshipped Shiva, the giver of enjoyment and liberation, O sage.
Krishna himself constantly performed the worship of Shiva alone on Badari, best of mountains, for a period of seven months.
From Shankara, who was pleased, the Lord obtained many divine boons and brought the whole world under his control.
Brahma said: Listen gladly, Narada, to the excellent deeds of Shankara; out of affection for you I shall tell them — they destroy the great sins.
His son Pradyumna, dear one, always worshipped Shiva, and other eminent descendants of Krishna, Samba and the rest, were worshippers of Shiva.
Jarasandha was a great Shaiva, as were the kings of his line; Nimi was a Shaiva, and Janaka and his sons were worshippers of Shiva.
Worship was performed also by Nala, son of Virasena, who in a former birth was a Bhil in the forest, a protector of travellers.
Long ago near a shrine of Hara he protected an ascetic, and was himself devoured in the night by tigers and other beasts; he died through that righteousness.
By the power of that merit the Bhil became Nala, an emperor, a great king, the beloved of Damayanti.
Thus, dear sinless one, I have told you what you asked, the divine deeds of Shankara; what else do you wish to ask?
Vishnu together with Rama (Lakshmi) performed the worship of Shiva, and by the grace of the supreme lord obtained all his desires.
I too, the Grandsire, am a worshipper of Shiva; by his grace alone, dear one, I am ever the creator of the universe.
My sons, the great sages, worship Shiva daily, and the other sages too are worshippers of Shiva.
You, Narada, are especially a worshipper of Shiva; the seven sages headed by Vasishtha are worshippers of Shiva.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, fourth book, the Kotirudra Samhita, chapter 38: the exposition of the greatness of the Shivaratri vow. The sages said: You are blessed, you have fulfilled your purpose, your life is fruitful, dear one, since you let us hear the auspicious story of Maheshvara.
Those versed in the Jabala Shruti speak of ten Shaiva vows; these vows should always be performed with care by the twice-born.
On every eighth lunar day one should diligently eat only at night; on the Kalashtami especially, Hari, eating by day is to be given up.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, Vishnu, eating by day is to be given up; on that of the dark fortnight one should eat at night after worshipping me, Hari.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight one should eat at night; but on the dark fourteenth, those under Shiva's vow should not do so.
On Mondays in both fortnights, Vishnu, those devoted to Shiva should take care to eat only at night.
In all these vows Shaivas should be fed with care, according to one's means, O best of brahmins, for the completion of the vow.
These vows should be observed as a rule by the twice-born; brahmins who abandon these vows become thieves.
Those skilled in the path of liberation should observe them as a rule. Fourfold, it is said, is what leads to liberation:
the worship of Shiva, the japa of Rudra, fasting in a Shiva temple, and death in Varanasi — this is the eternal liberation.
The eighth day, Monday, and the fourteenth of the dark fortnight — these please Shiva; there is no need to deliberate on it.
Though the truth of it has been heard by many sages, Suta, our doubt has not gone; so we tell it to you.
Of all four, Hari, the Shivaratri vow is the most powerful; therefore those who seek the fruit of enjoyment and liberation should observe it.
There is nothing other than this vow that brings good to men; this vow is the highest means of dharma for all —
for those free of desire and those with desires, for all men, for all classes and stages of life, and for women and children, Hari,
for male and female servants, for the gods and others as well — for all embodied beings this excellent vow is beneficial.
In the dark fortnight of Magha the night is declared especially great; it should be taken where it extends through midnight, and it destroys ten million murders.
What should be done on that day, Keshava, beginning from dawn — listen with attention; I tell it to you gladly.
Rising at dawn, the wise man, filled with supreme joy, should tirelessly perform his daily duties, bathing and the rest.
Then going to a Shiva temple and worshipping according to rule, having bowed to Shiva, he should duly make his vow of intent:

God of gods, Mahadeva, Nilakantha, salutation to you. I wish to perform your Shivaratri vow, O God.

Having made this vow of intent, he should gather the materials of worship; and at a linga in a good place, one renowned in the Agamas,
going there himself at night and arranging the excellent rite, in a clean spot to the south or west of Shiva,
he should place those materials for worship in Shiva's presence; then that best of men should bathe there again according to rule.
Putting on a clean garment and a clean undergarment, and sipping water three times, he should begin the worship.
With whatever material belongs to each mantra he should perform the worship; the worship of Hara must not be done without mantras.
Having performed the worship in the first watch with songs, instruments and dances full of devotion, the wise man should repeat the mantra.
If he knows the mantras, he should then make an excellent earthen linga; having done his daily rites, he should afterwards worship the earthen linga.
First making the earthen linga, he should then install it, and please the bull-bannered god with hymns of many kinds.
The account of the greatness arising from the vow should be read by the wise and heard by the best of devotees, wishing for the completion of the vow.
In all four watches, the four forms should be worshipped in order, from invocation to dismissal;
By what vow may devotees obtain enjoyment and liberation — tell us that in particular, disciple of Vyasa; salutation to you.
and a vigil should be kept lovingly, with a great festival. At dawn, bathing again, he should install and worship Shiva there.
Then, having completed the vow, with bowed shoulders and folded hands, bowing to him again and again, he should entreat Shambhu:

The observance I undertook by your command, Mahadeva, I now conclude, master; the vow has been completed, unsurpassed.
shivpurana:8:38.43	By this vow, performed according to my ability, O lord of gods, be pleased today, Sharva, and have mercy upon me.
Offering a handful of flowers to Shiva, he should give gifts according to rule; bowing to Shiva, he should conclude that observance.
According to his means he should feed Shaiva brahmins, and ascetics especially, satisfy them well, and then eat himself.
How worship is to be performed watch by watch by the best devotees, Hari, especially on Shivaratri — that I shall tell you.
In the first watch, Hari, one should worship the installed earthen linga with supreme devotion and many fine offerings.
Hara should always be worshipped first with the five substances; each substance should be offered separately with its own mantra.
Having offered each substance he should pour a stream of water; afterwards the wise man should wash the substances off with streams of water.
Suta said: Rightly have you asked, best of sages, compassionate as you are. Remembering Shiva's lotus feet, I shall tell it as I have heard it.
Reciting the mantra a hundred and eight times with the stream of water, he should worship Shiva there, who is beyond qualities yet takes the form of qualities.
He should worship the bull-bannered god with the mantra given by his guru; otherwise he should worship Sadashiva with the name-mantra.
Worship of Shambhu, the supreme self, should be done with fragrant sandal paste, unbroken rice grains and black sesame.
With flowers, hundred-petalled lotuses and oleanders, he should offer the flowers to Shankara with eight name-mantras.
Bhava, Sharva, Rudra, Pashupati, Ugra, Mahan, Bhima and Ishana — these are they.
He should worship Shiva with these names preceded by "Shri" and in the dative; then incense, the lamp, and after that the food offering.
In the first watch the wise man should have cooked food prepared as the offering; having given the arghya and a bilva fruit, he should offer betel.
Then salutation, meditation, and japa of the guru's mantra are prescribed; otherwise he should please Shankara with the five-syllabled mantra.
Then, showing the cow-gesture, he should make a libation with pure water, and arrange for five brahmins to be fed according to his means.
A great festival should be held as long as the watch lasts here; then, offering him the fruit of the worship, he should conclude it.
As you ask, so did the Creator ask, and Hari and Shiva's consort too, of Shankara.
Again, in the second watch he should make the vow of intent; or, having made it once only, he should perform the worship in the same way.
Worshipping with the former substances, he should offer the stream of water; reciting the mantra twice as many times as before, he should worship Shiva.
With the former sesame and barley, and with lotuses, he should worship Shiva, and above all with bilva leaves he should worship the supreme lord.
The arghya with a citron and the food offering of sweet rice; the repetitions of the mantra double those before, Janardana.
Then he should make the resolve to feed brahmins, and do everything else in the same way until the end of the second watch.
When the third watch arrives he should worship as before, with wheat in place of barley and flowers of the arka plant,
with various incenses and lamps of many kinds, and with offerings of cakes and vegetables of many kinds, Vishnu.
Having done this, he should perform the arati rite with camphor, give an arghya with a pomegranate, and do double the japa.
Then the resolve to feed brahmins, with fees; and he should hold the festival as before until the end of the watch.
When the fourth watch arrives he should dismiss that (third watch's worship), and, performing the preliminary rites again, carry out the worship according to rule,
At a certain time they asked the supreme self: "By what vow are you pleased, so that you grant enjoyment and liberation?"
with black gram, millet, green gram or the seven grains, and with shankhi flowers and bilva leaves he should worship the supreme lord.
There he should give a food offering of various sweets, or else please Sadashiva with food made of black gram.
He should give the arghya with a banana fruit, Hari, or else give the arghya to Shiva with various fruits.
That best of men should do the japa of the mantra twice as much as before, and the wise man should make the resolve to feed brahmins according to his means.
He should pass the time devoutly with songs, instruments and dances, and great festivities with devotees, until the dawn breaks.
When dawn has come, he should bathe again and worship Shiva, and perform his own ablution with offerings of many kinds.
Gifts of many kinds and food of various sorts should be given to brahmins and ascetics, according to the number of watches.
Bowing to Shankara, he should then offer a handful of flowers, and the discerning man should entreat him with these mantras, praising him well:

I am yours, my life is in you, my mind is ever in you, Mrida; knowing this, O treasury of compassion, do as is fitting.

Having offered the handful of flowers thus, he should receive the tilaka mark and blessings from the brahmins, and then dismiss Shambhu.
From one who has performed the vow thus, Hara is never far. Its fruit cannot be told; there is nothing I would not give.
Even if this supreme vow is performed without effort, the seed of liberation is born in him; there is no doubt of it.
Men should perform the vow devoutly every month; afterwards, performing the rite of concluding it, one gains the complete fruit.
Surely by the performance of this vow, I, Shiva, remover of all sorrow, grant enjoyment and liberation and every fruit desired.
Suta said: Having heard these words of Shiva, most beneficial and wonderful, Vishnu returned to his abode; and afterwards this excellent vow was practised among people who sought their own good.
At one time Keshava told this divine Shivaratri vow, which gives enjoyment and liberation, to Narada.
Shiva said: I have many vows which give enjoyment and liberation; among them the chief are to be known as ten in number.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, fourth book, the Kotirudra Samhita, chapter 39: the concluding rite of the Shivaratri vow. The sages said: Tell us the rite for concluding the Shivaratri vow, by performing which Shankara surely becomes pleased in person.
Diligently placing the image of Shiva's consort on the left and mine on the right, he should worship at night.
There he should choose a pure teacher together with officiating priests, and with their leave perform the worship of Shiva devoutly.
He should keep vigil at night, performing the worship of each watch; the observer of the vow should pass the whole night in song, dance and the like.
Having thus worshipped according to rule and given satisfaction, at dawn he should worship again and then perform the fire offering according to rule.
According to his means he should perform the Prajapatya rite; he should feed brahmins lovingly and give gifts devoutly.
Adorning the officiating priests and their wives with clothes, ornaments and jewellery according to rule, he should give gifts to each separately.
He should give the teacher a cow with its calf, duly furnished with its accessories, saying, "May Shiva be pleased with me."
Then he should present to the teacher that image with the pot, clothed, seated on a bull, together with all its ornaments.
Then with folded hands and bowed shoulders, in great love, his voice choked, he should entreat the god Maheshana, the great lord:

God of gods, Mahadeva, kind to those who seek refuge, by this vow, lord of gods, have mercy on me.
shivpurana:8:39.2	Suta said: Hear devoutly, O sages, and with respect, the concluding rite, by the performance of which the vow is surely made complete.
shivpurana:8:39.20	I have performed this vow according to my devotion, Shiva; whatever is lacking, may it reach completeness by your grace, Shankara.

Having thus offered a handful of flowers to Shiva, the supreme self, he should then bow and make his prayer again.
For one who has performed the vow in this way nothing is lacking; he then obtains the fulfilment his heart desires, without doubt.
The auspicious Shivaratri vow should be observed for fourteen years: one meal on the thirteenth day and a fast on the fourteenth.
When the day of Shivaratri comes, having completed the daily rite, one should go to a Shiva temple and worship according to rule.

Then he should carefully have a divine mandala made there, known in the three worlds by the name Gauritilaka. In its centre he should draw the divine Lingatobhadra mandala, or else arrange a Sarvatobhadra within the pavilion.
Pots should be set up there with the Prajapatya designation, auspicious, covered with cloth, with fruits and with fees.
They should be carefully placed around the mandala, and in the centre one pot of gold, or another kind, should be set.
There the observer of the vow should make a golden image of Shambhu together with Uma, of one pala of gold, or half that, or according to his means.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, fourth book, the Kotirudra Samhita, chapter 40: the description of the greatness of the Shivaratri vow. The sages said: Suta, hearing your words we have attained supreme joy; tell us lovingly and in detail about that excellent vow.
As fate would have it, he found nothing at all that day; the sun set, and he fell into distress.
Austerities of many kinds and japas without number do not equal this Shivaratri vow.
Therefore those who seek their good should perform this most auspicious divine Shivaratri vow, which always gives enjoyment and liberation.
I have told you all of this auspicious Shivaratri vow, famed as the king of vows; what else do you wish to hear?

What am I to do, where am I to go? I have got nothing today. What will become of the children at home, and of my parents?

Reflecting thus, the hunter went near a lake and stationed himself where the path goes down to the water.

Thinking thus, the Bhil climbed a tree called bilva and stayed there, having taken water with him.
When will some creature come? When shall I kill it? With this thought he waited there, tormented by hunger and thirst.
That night, in the first watch, a doe came there, thirsty and timid, leaping about.
Seeing her, he was thrilled, and to kill her quickly fitted an arrow to his bow.
As he did this, water and bilva leaves fell down below, where there was a Shiva linga.
Who performed this excellent vow here long ago, Suta, and what excellent fruit did he gain by performing it even in ignorance?
Thus the worship of Shiva for the first watch took place, and by its glory his sin melted away then and there.
Hearing that sound there, the doe, frightened, saw the hunter and, alarmed, spoke these words.
The doe said: "What do you mean to do, hunter? Tell me the truth." Hearing the doe's words, the hunter replied.
The hunter said: "My family is hungry today; I will kill you and feed them." Hearing those cruel words and seeing that fierce villain,
she thought, "What shall I do, where shall I go? I must devise some means." Reflecting thus, she said these words.
The doe said: "If by my flesh you are made happy, what greater merit could there be for this useless body? I am blessed; there is no doubt.
The merit that arises here for one who does a kindness cannot be told even in hundreds of years.
But my little ones are all at my dwelling now; I will hand them over to my sister, or else to my mate, and come back.
Know that my words are not false, forest-dweller; I will come back here to you, without doubt.
By truth the earth stands, by truth the ocean, by truth the streams of water flow; on truth everything is founded."
Suta said: Listen, all you sages; I shall tell you the ancient history of a Nishada, which destroys all sins.
Suta said: When the hunter, though told this by her, did not believe her words, she, astonished and afraid, spoke again.
The doe said: "Listen, hunter, I will tell you and swear an oath: if, having gone home, I do not come back to you,
then the sin of a brahmin who sells the Veda or neglects the three twilight rites, of women who defy their husbands' command in their deeds,
the sin of the ungrateful, the sin of one turned against Hari, the sin of the treacherous, the sin of transgressing dharma,
the sin of one who betrays trust and of the deceiver — with that sin let me be stained, if I do not come back."
When the doe had sworn these and many other oaths and stood there, the hunter trusted her and said, "Go home."
The doe, delighted, drank water and went to her dwelling; meanwhile the first watch passed for him without sleep.
Her sister, another doe, thinking of her and searching for her track, came there seeking water.
Seeing her, the Bhil drew his arrow himself, and as before water and leaves fell upon Shiva.
By that, incidentally, the worship of the great-souled Shambhu for the second watch took place, bringing happiness to the hunter.
Long ago there was a Bhil in the forest named Gurudruha, a family man, strong and cruel, given to cruel deeds.
Seeing him, the doe said, "What are you doing, forest-dweller?" He told her as before, and hearing it the doe spoke again.
The doe said: "I am blessed; listen, hunter — my bearing of a body is fruitful, for with this impermanent body a kindness will be done.
But my young ones, little fawns, are at home; I will hand them to my mate and come back."
The hunter said: "I do not believe what you say; I will kill you, no doubt of it." Hearing this, the doe spoke, swearing by Hari.
The doe said: "Listen, hunter, I will tell you: if I do not come back — whoever wavers from his word loses his merit by it —
the man who leaves his wedded wife and goes to another, who transgresses Vedic dharma and follows an invented path,
who, devoted to Vishnu, reviles Shiva, who on the anniversary of his parents' death lets it pass empty,
who, after causing distress, speaks again — with that sin let me be stained, if I do not come back."
Suta said: Addressed thus by her, the hunter said to the doe, "Go," and the doe drank water and went joyfully to her dwelling.

realizing the delay, he grew anxious and intent on searching for them; in that watch he saw a buck that had come along the path to the water.
Seeing that plump buck, the forest-dweller was delighted, fitted an arrow to his bow and set about killing it.
As he did so, some bilva leaves, by the force of his destiny, O brahmins, fell upon Shiva.

Hearing that sound, the buck said, "What are you doing?" The hunter replied, "I will kill you for the sake of my family."
Hearing the hunter's words, the buck, glad at heart, at once spoke these words to the hunter.
The buck said: "I am blessed, I am well-fed, and you will be satisfied today. Everything is wasted for one whose body is not used for kindness.
He who has the ability and yet does no kindness — that ability is wasted, and in the next world he goes to hell.
But having handed my young ones to their mother and comforted them all, I will come back."
Addressed thus by him, the hunter was greatly astonished in his heart; a little purified in mind, his heap of sins destroyed, he spoke.
From childhood he had done nothing good here, and a long time passed for that wicked man in the forest.
The hunter said: "Everyone who came here spoke as you do and went away; the deceivers have not come back even now.
You too, caught in danger, will go off with a lie; how, deer, am I to keep myself alive today?"
The buck said: "Listen, hunter, I will tell you: there is no falsehood in me. By truth the whole cosmos, moving and unmoving, stands.
He whose speech is false loses his merit in an instant. Still, hear my true vow, Bhil:
the sin of intercourse at twilight or by day, of eating on Shivaratri, of false witness, of stealing a deposit, of a brahmin who neglects the twilight rites,
of one whose mouth is without Shiva's name, of one who, though able, does no kindness, of breaking bilva on a festival day, of eating forbidden food,
of one who eats food without worshipping Shiva and without wearing ash — let the sin of these be mine, if I do not come back."
Suta said: Hearing his words, the hunter said, "Go quickly and return." Told thus by the hunter, the buck drank water and went.
They all met there at their dwelling, having made their vows, and hearing the whole story from one another fully,
bound by the noose of truth, they resolved that they must go; comforting the young ones there, they were eager to go.
Once the auspicious Shivaratri came there, but the wicked man, living deep in the great forest, did not know it.
The elder doe there said to her mate: "Without you, deer, how will the young ones survive here?
It was I who made the promise there first, lord; therefore I must go, and you two stay here."
Hearing her words, the younger said: "I am your servant; today I will go, and you stay."
Hearing this, the buck said: "I will go there; you two stay here, for the young are protected by their mother."
Hearing their lord's words, they did not accept them as right, and said lovingly to their husband, "Shame on life in widowhood!"
Comforting the young ones and entrusting them to their neighbours, they all went quickly to where the excellent hunter was.
The young ones too, seeing them go, all followed, thinking, "Whatever fate is theirs, let it be ours too."
Seeing them, the hunter was delighted and fitted an arrow to his bow, and again water and leaves fell upon Shiva.
By that the auspicious worship of the fourth watch took place, and all his sin was burned to ashes in an instant.
The two does and the buck said: "Quickly, best of hunters, make our bodies meaningful; show us this kindness."

Hearing their words, the hunter was filled with wonder; by the power of the worship of Shiva he gained knowledge hard to attain.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, fourth book, the Kotirudra Samhita, chapter 41: the exposition of liberation. The sages said: You have spoken of what is called liberation; what happens in it here? Tell us what the state is like there.
Vishnu did not know it, nor did Brahma; Kumara and the others did not know it, nor did Narada;
nor Shuka son of Vyasa, nor Vyasa and the lords of sages, nor all the gods before them, nor the Vedas and shastras.
It is called truth, knowledge and the infinite, being-consciousness-bliss; beyond qualities, without limiting adjuncts, imperishable, pure and stainless.
It is not red, nor yellow, nor white, nor blue; not short, nor long, nor gross, nor subtle.
That from which words turn back together with the mind, not having reached it — that alone is declared the supreme, the Brahman called Shiva.
Just as space is all-pervading, so is this all-pervading: beyond maya, the supreme self, beyond the pairs of opposites, free of envy.
Its attainment surely comes here through the dawning of the knowledge of Shiva, or through the worship of Shiva with a subtle mind, O brahmins, for the good.
Knowledge is hard in the world, while worship is held to be easy; therefore, best of men, worship Shiva, even for the sake of liberation.
Shiva, whose nature is knowledge, the supreme giver of liberation, is won by worship; through devotion alone many perfected ones joyfully attained the supreme liberation.
Devotion to Shambhu is the mother of knowledge and always gives liberation and enjoyment; by his grace it is easily attained, its mark the sprouting of true love.
Suta said: Liberation is declared to be fourfold; listen, I shall tell you. It removes the afflictions of worldly existence and gives supreme bliss.
That devotion should be known as of two kinds, with qualities and without qualities, O brahmins; whether prescribed or spontaneous, whichever is superior is deemed the higher.
